title: What Do We Give Agni? — Ṛtāvan Said Three Times
synthesis:
This sūkta begins where [[1.76]] began, with a question about giving, and then does something the previous hymn did not: it answers by repeating one epithet until the answer is unmistakable.

*Kathā dāśema agnaye* — how shall we give to {{agni}}? What speech, loved by the gods, is spoken to the shining one? The first verse gives its own reply in the second half: he who among mortals is *amṛta*, deathless, *ṛtāvā*, possessed of {{ṛta}} — the order by which things run true — and *hotā yajiṣṭhaḥ*, the caller who sacrifices best. That is the answer. You give to the one who keeps the order, and what you give is the giving itself.

The second verse repeats *ṛtāvā* and adds what it is for. Him who is *śaṃtama* in the rites, most benign, and *ṛtāvā hotā* — bring him near with *namas*, with the homage that bends. And then the reason, stated as a piece of information rather than praise: when Agni goes to the gods on a mortal's behalf, *sa ca bodhāti manasā yajāti*, he knows them, and he sacrifices with mind. The intermediary is not a conveyor belt. He understands the parties on both sides, which is why he can be trusted with the errand.

The third verse piles up what Agni is, in short clauses that do not connect grammatically so much as accumulate. *Sa hi kratuḥ sa maryaḥ sa sādhuḥ* — he is *kratu*, the resolve that gets things done; he is a young man; he is one who brings things to completion. He becomes like a *mitra*, a friend and ally, and is *rathīḥ adbhutasya*, charioteer of the wondrous. Then the social fact: *taṃ medheṣu prathamaṃ devayantīḥ viśaḥ upa bruvate dasmam ārīḥ* — at the rites, the god-seeking Ārya clans speak to him first, to him the wonder-worker. First, before any other god. That is not a claim about rank; it is a description of what people actually do, and it is the same practice that put Agni at the head of the collection.

The fourth verse asks for the reception of the offering and then widens. May Agni, *nṛtamaḥ* — most manly among men — and *riśādāḥ*, destroyer of hostility, come to our songs and to our *dhīti*, our formed thought, with help. And with him: those *maghavānaḥ*, the liberal patrons, strongest, *vājaprasūtāḥ*, impelled by *vāja*, the strength that a rite generates — may they too take pleasure in the *manman*, the composed hymn. The patrons are inside the prayer, not outside it. A rite has people who pay for it, and this verse asks that they be moved as well.

The fifth verse signs the work. *Evā agnir gotamebhir ṛtāvā viprebhir astoṣṭa jātavedāḥ* — thus Agni, *ṛtāvā*, Jātavedas, has been praised by the Gotamas, the inspired ones. Third and last occurrence of *ṛtāvā*, and it is now the settled name of the one who has been described. What follows is the return: may he swell *dyumna*, brilliance, in them; he goes to *vāja*, to *puṣṭi*, to nourishment, *joṣam ā cikitvān* — perceiving, and taking pleasure. The hymn that opened not knowing what to give ends by describing the giver enjoying what came back.
practice:
The question in the first line is the ordinary one: *kathā dāśema* — how are we to give? Not what to give. The hymn assumes the materials are available and doubts the manner, which is where most people actually stand.

What it settles on is *ṛtāvan*, three times: verse 1, verse 2, verse 5. The word is a possessive — one who has *ṛta*, who holds the order of things. Agni is worth giving to because he keeps that order, and by extension the giving is worth doing because it participates in the same order. This is the vocabulary a reciter already carries: *ṛta* is the truth of a thing, the regularity of the seasons, and the correct performance of a rite, all under one word, and the Ṛgveda does not treat these as three meanings. [[1.2]].8 puts three forms of it in a single line about Mitra and Varuṇa; here one form does the same work three times across a short hymn.

Verse 3 records something about ordinary observance that no doctrine states: the clans *speak to Agni first*. Before Indra, before Varuṇa, before whoever the day's rite is for. That habit is why the Anukramaṇī names Agni in the dedication of 230 of the Ṛgveda's 1,028 sūktas, why eight of the ten maṇḍalas open with him, and why in a modern pūjā the lamp is lit before anything else is offered. The verse describes the practice; the arrangement of the collection reflects it.

Verse 4 is the one worth carrying into a household. It asks for the offering to be received, and in the same breath asks that the *maghavānaḥ*, the people whose generosity paid for the rite, be stirred by the hymn. A rite is not only between a worshipper and a god. Somebody bought the ghee. The Ṛgveda puts them inside the prayer rather than thanking them afterward, and a family that supports a temple, a teacher or a recitation is standing where those patrons stand.

The closing verse names the singers as *gotamāḥ*, plural. Whatever the individual authorship, the tradition transmits these as a family's work, and the last verse of a Gotama hymn regularly says so.
disagreements:
Verse 3 is where the readings diverge most sharply, on three short words: *sa hi kratuḥ sa maryaḥ sa sādhuḥ*. Sāyaṇa takes *marya* and *sādhu* as a paired opposition — destroyer and reviver, "killer or extirpator of all and the producer" — and Wilson prints exactly that: "he is the destroyer and reviver (of all things)." Griffith reads the words at face value: "he is mental power, a man, and perfect." The Sanskrit supports Griffith more easily; *marya* is a common word for a young man. But Sāyaṇa's reading is not arbitrary, and it makes verse 3 a statement about Agni's double capacity rather than a list of compliments.

The last verse divides them almost as far. Wilson has Agni giving the singers "the bright Soma to drink, along with the sacrificial food"; Griffith has him augmenting "splendour and vigour" in them. The padapāṭha reads *saḥ eṣu dyumnam pīpayat*, he shall make *dyumna* swell in them, which is closer to Griffith; Wilson's soma appears to come from Sāyaṇa's expansion rather than from the words.

On verse 2, Sāyaṇa notes that *manasā*, with the mind, is read by some as *namasā*, with reverence, assuming a transposition of syllables — a genuine textual observation, and one he records without choosing.
